title: Milk to curd
hookLine: milk becomes curd, then butter: continuity without a fixed thing (Milinda, Book 2)

cards: A baby photo, propped on a shelf. Someone tiny on their back, not yet able to hold up their own head. Is that the grown person who walks past it every morning?
The quick answer is yes. But that baby had no words, none of the grown person's memories, hands a fraction of the size. So in what sense is it the same one?
Nagasena puts exactly this to the king, and the king's first answer is no: that baby was someone else. Nagasena shows him what that answer would cost, and then he reaches into a kitchen.

teach.h: IF THE BABY WAS SOMEONE ELSE...
teach.b: First, the cost of saying no. If the baby and the grown king are simply two different people, Nagasena says, then the king had no mother, no father, no teacher at all.

The boy who goes to school would be one person and the one who finishes his learning another. The one who does a wrong would be different from the one who answers for it. The king asks what Nagasena would say instead.

I was that tender baby, Nagasena says, and I am this grown man, held together as one by dependence on this same body, one moment depending on the one before. Third, the kitchen. Milk is taken from the cow.
After a while it turns to curd; from curd, butter; from butter, ghee. Would it be right to say the milk is the same as the curd, or the butter, or the ghee? No, says the king, but they came from it.

Just so, says Nagasena: one state arises, another passes away, and the line runs on, neither the same nor another. Fourth, why a kitchen. Nobody stands over a pot of curd arguing whether it's still the milk.
They know it came from the milk and wouldn't exist without it.
The milk didn't hand over some hidden essence. It changed, all the way through. So the baby in the photo isn't a stranger, and isn't a frozen self either.
It's milk, and the person looking at the photo is the butter.

how: Buddhist teachers often use Nagasena's milk, curd, butter and ghee image to explain how a life continues without a fixed self: each state arises from the one before.

o: milk kept fresh and unchanged for a long time
milk changed into something new, yet from the milk
an offering of butter poured into a fire

games.q: milk to curd: tap the pairs.
p: turns, after a while, to curd
held as one through the same body
not the milk, but came from it

s: Nagasena says the baby and the grown king are two different people
that was the king's first answer. Nagasena shows its cost and says he himself was the baby and is the grown man.
in the image, milk becomes curd, then butter, then ghee
and none of them is simply the milk, yet all came from it.
Nagasena says the milk passes a hidden essence to the curd
his point is change all the way through: one state arises from the one before.

games.q: you're the king. Nagasena asks: when milk has become curd, then butter, then ghee, is the ghee the same thing as the milk?
o: no, it has nothing to do with the milk.
no, but it came from the milk.
games.why: the king says it isn't the milk, but it came from it. just so, says Nagasena: the line of a life runs on, neither the same nor another.

practice: Look for something in the middle of becoming, tea cooling, a plant leaning toward the window, light shifting across the floor, and watch it for a moment.
Then let your hands rest in your lap: once they were small enough to grip one finger, and now they're changed all the way through. Nothing needs to be held still.

wordCard.voice: Curd. Nagasena's kitchen image: not the milk, and not something else either, but what came from it.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: curd. the second stage in Nagasena's milk image.

carryVoice: Your line: milk to butter. Changed all the way through, and still from the same milk. Day eight hundred seventy-one, done.

sources.ref: Milindapanha, Book 2 (neither the same nor another: the baby and the man; milk, curd, butter, ghee)
